blocks.text: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a node based data structure that keeps its elements in sorted order while supporting insert, search, and delete in O(log n) time, as long as the tree stays reasonably balanced.

Arrays and hash sets each solve only half of this problem. A sorted array supports fast search but slow inserts. A hash set supports fast inserts and search but throws away all ordering information. A BST is the structure that gives you both, fast lookups and a structure you can walk in sorted order at any time.
This is why BSTs sit at the foundation of C++'s std::set and std::map, of database indexes, and of a large family of interview questions that ask you to reason about ordered data.

items: Insert: add a new value while keeping the tree sorted
Search: check whether a value exists
Delete: remove a value while keeping the tree valid
Order statistics: find the smallest element greater than or equal to x, or the kth smallest element overall, something a hash set cannot do at all

blocks.text: This lesson builds a BST from scratch in C++, walks through why deletion is the operation everyone gets wrong first, explains why an unbalanced BST quietly degrades into a linked list, and shows why competitive programmers almost never hand roll one of these in an interview once std::set is available.

content.title: 1. The Problem: Why Arrays and Hash Sets Fall Short

blocks.text: Suppose you need a collection of numbers that supports fast search, and you occasionally need to know the smallest element greater than or equal to some value x. Two obvious choices are a sorted array and a hash set. Both fall short in their own way.
A sorted array

A sorted array gives you O(log n) search using binary search, and it naturally supports range and order queries. The problem is insertion and deletion. Adding or removing an element in the middle of a sorted array requires shifting every element after it, which costs O(n) in the worst case.
A hash set

unordered_set flips the tradeoff completely. Insert, search, and delete are all O(1) on average. But a hash set throws away all ordering information by design, the whole point of hashing is to scatter values so lookups are fast, not to keep them near their neighbors.

items: No sorted iteration, walking a hash set gives values in an unspecified order
No range queries, there is no efficient way to ask for all values between x and y
No order statistics, there is no way to ask for the kth smallest value without a full scan

blocks.text: A Binary Search Tree is the structure built specifically to close this gap: it keeps elements sorted like an array, but reorganizes itself as a tree so insert, search, and delete all stay close to O(log n) instead of degrading to O(n).
Every Binary Search Tree obeys exactly one rule, applied recursively at every node:
For any node, every value in its left subtree is smaller than the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is greater than the node's value.
This has to hold not just for a node's immediate children, but for the entire left and right subtrees, all the way down. A single violation anywhere breaks the invariant for the whole tree.

blocks.caption: Every node splits the tree into a smaller left half and a larger right half
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762809-774775819.png

This one rule is what turns search into a sequence of binary decisions. At each node you only need one comparison to know which half of the tree the answer could possibly be in, exactly the same idea as binary search on a sorted array, except the array has been reshaped into a tree.
A node in a BST needs just three fields: its value, and a pointer to its left and right child.

Duplicate values need a policy decision up front. Some implementations disallow them, some push equal values to one side consistently, commonly the right, and some use a separate count field on the node instead of inserting a second physical node. std::multiset solves this for you automatically, which is one more reason it is preferred in practice.

Both insert and search follow the same walk down the tree, only insert keeps going until it finds an empty spot to attach a new node, while search stops the moment it finds a match or runs out of tree.
Insert

Starting at the root, compare the new value against the current node. Go left if it is smaller, go right if it is larger, and repeat until you fall off the tree, that empty spot is exactly where the new node belongs.
Search
Search follows the identical comparison logic, except it stops as soon as it finds an exact match, or returns nullptr once it falls off the tree without finding one.

Both operations only ever touch one path from the root to a leaf, so their cost is proportional to the height of the tree, not the number of elements in it. This distinction between height and node count is the entire story of why BST performance can vary so much, covered in section 6.
In an interview setting, iterative versions of both functions are just as acceptable as recursive ones, and avoid adding a call stack frame per level, which matters if the tree could be very tall.

Deletion is the operation almost everyone gets wrong on a first attempt, because removing a node has to preserve the BST invariant for whatever is left behind. There are exactly three cases, based on how many children the node being deleted has.

items: Case 1, a leaf node: no children, simply remove it
Case 2, one child: splice the node out and reconnect its parent directly to its single child
Case 3, two children: the hard case, the node cannot simply be removed without breaking the tree for one of its subtrees

blocks.text: For the two child case, the standard fix is to replace the node's value with its in-order successor, the smallest value in its right subtree, found by walking left from the right child until there are no more left children. Once that value is copied up, the original successor node is deleted from the right subtree instead, and that deletion is guaranteed to fall into case 1 or case 2, never case 3 again.

blocks.caption: Deleting a two child node using its in-order successor, the smallest value in the right subtree
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762809-273185200.png

The in-order predecessor, the largest value in the left subtree, works exactly as well and is an equally valid choice. Either one preserves the invariant, since both sit exactly between the deleted value's old left and right subtrees.

The recursive call deleteNode(root->right, successor->val) is what makes this correct: it walks back down the right subtree to physically remove the successor node, which by construction has no left child, so that removal can never itself land in case 3.

content.title: 5. In-order Traversal: Sorted Output for Free

blocks.text: A direct consequence of the BST invariant is that visiting nodes in the order left subtree, current node, right subtree, known as an in-order traversal, produces every value in fully sorted order, with no sorting step required.

blocks.caption: In order traversal visits nodes left, node, right, producing sorted output automatically
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762809-273797962.png
blocks.alt: In-order Traversal: Sorted Output for Free

blocks.text: This is more than a curiosity. It gives you an O(n) way to dump a BST's contents as a sorted list, and it is the standard way to check whether a binary tree actually satisfies the BST invariant, build the in-order sequence and confirm it is strictly increasing.

This is also exactly what iterating a std::set in C++ does under the hood. A range based for loop over a set walks its underlying tree in order, which is why the values come out sorted without you asking for a sort.

content.title: 6. Why Balance Matters: When a BST Degrades to O(n)

blocks.text: Insert, search, and delete are all proportional to the tree's height, not to how many nodes it holds. For a balanced tree with n nodes, the height is O(log n). But nothing in the basic insert function shown earlier does anything to keep the tree balanced.

Insert values that already arrive in sorted order, say 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and the naive BST from section 3 will attach every new value as the right child of the previous one. The result is a structure with height n, every operation on it costs O(n), and it is, for all practical purposes, a linked list wearing a tree's name.

blocks.caption: Inserting sorted values in order produces a skewed chain instead of a balanced tree
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762810-490022361.png
blocks.alt: Why Balance Matters: When a BST Degrades to On

items: Balanced BST with n nodes, height is O(log n), every operation is O(log n)
Fully skewed BST with n nodes, height is O(n), every operation degrades to O(n)

blocks.text: This is not a rare edge case. Sorted or nearly sorted input shows up constantly in real data, IDs, timestamps, and already processed lists all tend to arrive in order, and a plain BST has no defense against it.

This is exactly why test cases for BST problems often construct the tree by inserting a sorted array directly, on purpose, to check whether a solution silently assumes a balanced shape that was never guaranteed.

content.title: 7. Self-Balancing BSTs: AVL and Red-Black Trees

blocks.text: The fix for the skew problem is to make the tree actively maintain a balance invariant as it changes, rather than hoping insertions happen to arrive in a good order. Trees that do this are called self-balancing, and the two most common variants are AVL trees and Red-Black trees.

Both work the same way conceptually. After an insert or delete, the tree checks whether its balance invariant still holds, and if it does not, it performs a rotation, a local restructuring of a few pointers that changes the tree's shape without violating the BST invariant, and repeats until the tree is balanced again.
The four rotation shapes, briefly

items: Left Left case: a single right rotation restores balance
Right Right case: a single left rotation restores balance
Left Right case: a left rotation on the left child, followed by a right rotation on the node itself
Right Left case: a right rotation on the right child, followed by a left rotation on the node itself

blocks.text: AVL versus Red-Black, the practical difference

items: AVL trees enforce a strict balance factor, the heights of any node's two subtrees can differ by at most one. This keeps the tree very close to perfectly balanced, giving slightly faster lookups, at the cost of more rotations on insert and delete.

Red-Black trees enforce a looser invariant based on coloring nodes red or black, allowing the tree to be somewhat less balanced in exchange for far fewer rotations. This tradeoff favors workloads with frequent insertions and deletions.

blocks.text: Neither of these needs to be implemented from scratch in most interview settings, understanding what problem rotations solve and being able to describe one is normally enough. What matters more is knowing which one shows up in the tools you already use.

C++'s std::set and std::map are backed by a Red-Black tree internally. This is exactly why competitive programmers and interview candidates reach for std::set instead of hand rolling a BST, you get guaranteed O(log n) operations without writing or debugging a single rotation.

content.title: 8. Order Statistics: Beyond What a Hash Set Can Do

blocks.text: A hash set answers exactly one question well: is this value present. An ordered structure like a balanced BST or std::set answers a much richer family of questions, because it always knows the relative order of its elements.

items: lower_bound(x): the smallest element greater than or equal to x
upper_bound(x): the smallest element strictly greater than x
Predecessor and successor: the element immediately before or after a given value
Range queries: every element between two bounds, walked in order
Kth smallest element: the element that would sit at position k if the whole set were sorted

blocks.text: None of these are possible on a plain hash set without scanning every element. On a BST they are all O(log n), or O(n) for a full range walk, because the tree already encodes the relative order of everything it holds.
Kth smallest, with an augmented tree

Finding the kth smallest element efficiently requires one small addition to a plain BST: store the size of each node's subtree alongside its value, updated on every insert and delete. With that extra field, you can decide which subtree the kth element lives in using simple arithmetic, without ever touching the elements one by one.

This augmented structure is often called an order statistics tree. C++'s standard library does not expose this directly through std::set, but policy based data structures in GCC's extension library provide an order_of_key and find_by_order pair of operations that do exactly this.

content.title: 9. Worked Example: std::set and std::multiset in Practice

blocks.text: In practice, almost nobody hand rolls a BST to solve a problem, they reach for std::set and get a Red-Black tree's guarantees for free. Here is a small dataset run through the operations from the previous section.
Start with the values 30, 10, 50, 20, 40 inserted into a std::set<int>.
The set stores these five values already sorted as 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, so iterating it prints them in that order with no sorting step. Then:

items: lower_bound(25) returns an iterator to 30, the smallest value that is at least 25
upper_bound(30) returns an iterator to 40, the smallest value strictly greater than 30
find(20) returns an iterator to 20 directly, an O(log n) lookup

blocks.text: A note on duplicates

std::set silently ignores an insert of a value that already exists, since a set can only hold one copy of each key. When duplicates are meaningful, for example counting how many times a value has appeared, std::multiset is the right tool instead.

One detail worth internalizing here: ms.erase(20) would remove every copy of 20 from the multiset, while ms.erase(ms.find(20)) removes exactly the one occurrence the iterator points to. Reaching for the wrong overload is a common source of bugs.

Every operation shown here, insert, find, lower_bound, upper_bound, erase, count, runs in O(log n) on both std::set and std::multiset, because both are backed by the same Red-Black tree under the hood.

Every operation's cost comes down to the height of the tree. The table below compares the same operations under a balanced tree, guaranteed by AVL, Red-Black, or std::set, against a worst case skewed tree built from a plain, unbalanced BST.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Balanced BST (AVL / Red-Black / std::set)","Skewed BST (worst case)"],"rows":[["Search","O(log n)","O(n)"],["Insert","O(log n)","O(n)"],["Delete","O(log n)","O(n)"],["In order traversal","O(n)","O(n)"],["Find minimum or maximum","O(log n)","O(n)"],["Kth smallest (augmented tree)","O(log n)","O(n)"],["Space","O(n)","O(n)"]]}

blocks.text: The gap between the two columns is the entire reason self-balancing trees exist. A plain BST gives no guarantee about which column you land in, it depends entirely on the order elements were inserted.
A plain BST is rarely the final answer in production code or in competitive programming. Once you understand the base structure, it helps to know the landscape of variants built on top of it.

items: Plain BST: the version built in this lesson, simple to implement, but with no protection against skew
AVL tree: self balancing via a strict height invariant, favors read heavy workloads
Red-Black tree: self balancing via a looser color based invariant, favors write heavy workloads, backs std::set and std::map
Treap: a BST that assigns each node a random priority and maintains heap order on priority alongside BST order on value, achieving balance probabilistically instead of through strict rotation rules
Order statistics tree: a BST augmented with subtree size, adding kth element and rank queries on top of the usual operations
B-tree: a wider, shallower generalization used by databases and filesystems, where each node holds several keys instead of just one, to reduce disk reads

blocks.text: In an interview, naming the right variant for a given constraint, write heavy versus read heavy, or worst case guarantees versus average case, matters more than being able to implement every one of them from scratch.
These problems cover the full range of BST fundamentals, from validating the invariant to combining it with order statistics.

blocks.text: Most BST bugs come from getting the delete operation wrong, or from silently assuming guarantees that only a self balancing tree actually provides.

items: Forgetting the two child delete case and simply unlinking the node, which silently drops an entire subtree instead of reattaching it through the in-order successor or predecessor
Assuming a BST is always balanced and therefore always O(log n). A plain BST gives no such guarantee, only self balancing variants or std::set actually do
Using unbounded recursion without considering stack depth on a skewed or adversarially ordered tree, where a chain of n nodes means n recursive frames
Not deciding a duplicate value policy up front, leading to inconsistent behavior between insert, search, and delete once repeated values show up
Mixing up strict and non strict comparisons, for example using less than or equal where the invariant expects strict less than, which silently allows values to drift to the wrong side
Forgetting to reassign the return value of a recursive insert or delete call back onto the parent's left or right pointer, which leaves the tree completely unchanged

content.title: 14. BST / Ordered Set vs Hash Set

blocks.text: The two structures optimize for different things, and knowing which capability you actually need decides which one belongs in your solution.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability","BST / std::set (ordered)","unordered_set (hash set)"],"rows":[["Average lookup, insert, delete","O(log n)","O(1) average"],["Worst case lookup, insert, delete","O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed","O(n) with many hash collisions"],["Iteration order","Sorted order for free","Unspecified, insertion or bucket order"],["Range queries between two bounds","Yes, efficient via lower_bound and upper_bound","No, requires a full scan"],["Kth smallest element","Yes, with order statistics augmentation","Not supported"],["Memory overhead per element","Pointers plus balance metadata","Hash table buckets plus load factor overhead"]]}

blocks.text: Reach for std::set or std::map whenever a problem needs sorted iteration, range queries, or order statistics. Reach for unordered_set or unordered_map whenever all you need is raw membership or key lookup speed and order genuinely does not matter.
Before moving on to segment trees, tries, or a full self balancing tree implementation, make sure the fundamentals below are second nature.

items: Can you state the BST invariant precisely, for every node, and explain why it makes search a sequence of binary decisions?
Can you implement insert, search, and delete from scratch, including all three delete cases, in under ten minutes?
Can you explain why the in-order successor, or predecessor, is always a safe replacement when deleting a node with two children?
Can you explain why insert and search are O(height) rather than always O(log n), and give an example input that produces a skewed tree?
Do you know what problem AVL and Red-Black trees solve, and that std::set and std::map are Red-Black tree backed in C++?
Can you list at least three things an ordered set can do that a hash set fundamentally cannot?

blocks.text: Once these six questions feel automatic, std::set and std::map stop being a black box and become a tool you understand from the inside out.
